claims.text: Rapid solidification of Co-free FeNiCrMn forms uniformly distributed nanoscale Mn-oxide precipitates such as Mn2O3.
Rapidly solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn has a fine, homogeneous grain structure.
Rapidly solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn has a high dislocation density.
The nanoscale Mn-oxide precipitates are concentrated at cellular or grain boundaries.
At low temperatures, the Mn-oxide precipitates impede dislocation slip and strengthen FeNiCrMn through Orowan looping.
The nanoscale precipitates favor deformation twinning at lower temperatures.
At high temperatures, the Mn-oxide precipitates exert Zener drag.
Precipitate pinning delays dynamic recovery and recrystallization in FeNiCrMn at elevated temperatures.
The combined low-temperature dislocation obstruction and high-temperature pinning govern the dynamic response and preserve a strength–ductility balance across strain rates.
Precipitate-bearing FeNiCrMn will have lower strain-rate sensitivity at high temperatures than precipitate-dissolved controls.
Precipitate-bearing FeNiCrMn will show a more gradual decline in yield strength with temperature than precipitate-dissolved controls.
The Mn-oxide precipitates will retain a stable morphology during elevated-temperature deformation.
Recrystallization will begin later in precipitate-bearing FeNiCrMn than in precipitate-dissolved controls.
A post-solidification thermal treatment can dissolve the nanoscale Mn-oxide precipitates and create an otherwise suitable control.
FeNiCrMn lacking the distinctive oxide distribution will exhibit conventional thermal softening and earlier dynamic recrystallization.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to rapidly solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn with a sufficiently uniform nanoscale precipitate population.
Substantial changes in precipitate volume fraction or morphology may make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
Grain-size effects may dominate over precipitate effects under some conditions.
The relative contributions of grain-boundary strengthening and precipitate strengthening have not been separated quantitatively.

Similar strength trends, strain-rate sensitivity, and recrystallization onset in retained-precipitate and dissolved-precipitate specimens would falsify the proposed controlling role of the precipitates.
